summary: This informational memo looks at how existing IETF presence mechanisms can be used to distribute GEOPRIV location objects. GEOPRIV scenarios need subscriptions and asynchronous notifications, and the document examines how presence protocols can supply those.

eli5.summary: Your location could be shared with people you approve, with updates when it changes. This document explores using presence systems to do that.

questions: how can location be distributed using presence
how does presence relate to location sharing
can presence protocols carry location information
subtitle: Using presence systems to share location information safely

tldr.problem: GEOPRIV (a standard for distributing location information with privacy controls) requires subscriptions and notifications to share location as it changes. Presence architectures (used in instant messaging) already solve the subscription and notification problem.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC shows how the entities in a GEOPRIV system (Location Generator, Location Server, Location Recipient) map onto presence system entities, and how presence protocols like XMPP and SIMPLE can carry location objects instead of just online status.
tldr.outcome: GEOPRIV can reuse the subscription, notification, expiration, and security mechanisms that presence protocols already provide, rather than inventing new infrastructure.

today: RFC 4079 is an informational memo showing the architectural applicability of presence to GEOPRIV location distribution. It does not define a protocol but rather demonstrates that existing presence mechanisms can be adapted for location sharing. Later GEOPRIV work has pursued this direction, with presence protocols serving as using protocols for GEOPRIV location objects.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
GEOPRIV is a standard for safely transmitting location information over the Internet with privacy controls. Location can be represented as coordinates (latitude and longitude), civil addresses, or other forms. GEOPRIV specifies a secure container that holds both location data and privacy policies governing who can see that information.

Presence (defined in RFC 2778) is a service used in instant messaging and real-time communications that lets people monitor each other's availability—whether someone is online, busy, idle, or away. Presence information is highly dynamic.

The RFC shows that presence and GEOPRIV share a common need: both must deliver updated information to interested parties as that information changes. Rather than design separate mechanisms for location distribution, GEOPRIV can reuse the proven subscription and notification architecture that presence systems have already developed.
sections.eli5: Location sharing and instant messaging have the same core problem: telling interested people about information that changes frequently. Since instant messaging has already solved this, location sharing can use the same tools.

sections.title: The GEOPRIV Framework and Presence Parallels
sections.content:
The GEOPRIV framework defines four primary entities:

  • Location Generator: The device or system that determines location (e.g., a GPS receiver).
  • Location Server: The server that receives and stores location information and enforces privacy policies.
  • Location Recipient: A user or system authorized to receive location information about a target.
  • Rule Holder: The entity (usually the target) that sets policies for who can see the location.

GEOPRIV specifies publication and notification interfaces: Location Generators publish location to the server, and the server notifies authorized recipients. This is fundamentally a subscription and notification architecture.

Presence systems have identical structure: a watcher (equivalent to a Location Recipient) subscribes to a presentity (equivalent to the GEOPRIV target). The presence server accepts the subscription, and when the presentity's status changes, it sends notifications to all watchers. Presence also includes mechanisms for expiring stale subscriptions, maintaining subscription identifiers, and using URIs to identify watchers and presentities.
sections.eli5: GEOPRIV has a person sharing their location, a server storing it with rules, and other people who want updates. Presence has the same structure: someone shares their status, a server manages it, and others get notified.

sections.title: Presence Protocols as GEOPRIV Using Protocols
sections.content:
IETF presence systems define several concrete protocols and data formats:

Common Profile for Presence (CPP): An abstract framework for presence operations including subscriptions, unsubscriptions, and fetches. CPP also defines subscription expiration (to prevent stale subscriptions), transaction IDs, and a URI scheme ("pres:") for identifying principals.

Presence Information Data Format (PIDF): An XML format for encoding presence state. PIDF includes a presentity's status, contact addresses, timestamps, and extensible fields for additional attributes.

Concrete protocols: XMPP (used in Jabber) and SIMPLE (SIP-based presence) both instantiate the CPP framework and can carry PIDF. Both have server components where presentities register, policies can be managed, and subscriptions are stored. XMPP and SIMPLE also define policy protocols (like XCAP) for provisioning authorization policies.

The RFC observes that these protocols solve many of GEOPRIV's harder problems: subscription management, subscription expiration, user identification, and secure policy enforcement. Rather than reinvent, GEOPRIV can specify presence protocols as "using protocols" that carry location objects. PIDF can be extended with location-specific fields to represent GEOPRIV data.
sections.eli5: Presence protocols already have all the pieces GEOPRIV needs: how to let people subscribe to information, how to send updates, how to time out old subscriptions, and how to enforce access rules.

sections.title: Using PIDF for Location Data
sections.content:
PIDF (Presence Information Data Format) is an XML-based format that represents the status of a presentity. It includes a status element and optional contact information, timestamps, and notes.

PIDF is designed to be extensible. The RFC notes that although the authors of PIDF envisioned geographical location as a possible presence attribute, the baseline PIDF specification does not define a location element.

However, PIDF can be extended to carry GEOPRIV location information. The existing PIDF structure already maps well to GEOPRIV requirements: location can be encoded as an additional element or attribute, and PIDF's existing security mechanisms (which mirror those of GEOPRIV) provide authentication, confidentiality, and integrity protection.

The RFC emphasizes that PIDF's security properties, defined in RFC 2779, align well with GEOPRIV's security requirements: mutual authentication of participants, confidentiality and integrity of information, and resistance to abuse.
sections.eli5: Presence already has an XML format for sharing information (PIDF). You can add a location field to it, and it inherits all the presence system's security protections.

sections.title: Security and Deployment
sections.content:
GEOPRIV information is extremely sensitive: revealing someone's location enables physical harm, stalking, and privacy violations. Presence information has similar sensitivity, and presence systems implement strong security mechanisms.

The presence security framework (RFC 2779) requires authentication of watchers, confidentiality and integrity protection of information, and mechanisms to prevent abuse. These mechanisms are directly applicable to GEOPRIV:

  • Authentication ensures that only authorized Location Recipients receive location information.
  • Confidentiality and integrity protection prevent eavesdropping and tampering.
  • Policy enforcement (via XCAP and similar mechanisms) allows the Rule Holder to specify fine-grained access control.

By reusing presence protocols, GEOPRIV inherits these security properties without needing to redesign security from scratch. However, GEOPRIV deployments must be careful to properly configure authentication and policy enforcement, as misconfigurations could expose location information.

The RFC also notes that GEOPRIV scenarios are not limited to cases where the Location Recipient actively solicits location; some scenarios involve unsolicited notifications. However, the subscription/notification framework of presence can be adapted to handle both active and passive scenarios.
sections.eli5: Location is very sensitive information, but presence systems already have strong security. If GEOPRIV uses presence, it gets those protections for free.
